content: Carbonic anhydrase 1 (CA1) is an enzyme encoded by the CA1 gene in humans. Carbonic anhydrases (CAs) are a large family of zinc metalloenzymes that catalyze the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide. These enzymes are involved in various biological processes, including cellular respiration, calcification, acid-base balance, bone resorption, and the production of aqueous humor, cerebrospinal fluid, saliva, and gastric acid. They exhibit significant diversity in their tissue distribution and subcellular localization. The CA1 gene is closely linked to the CA2 and CA3 genes on chromosome 8. It encodes a cytosolic protein that is most abundantly found in erythrocytes (red blood cells). Transcript variants of CA1 that utilize alternative polyadenylation sites have been described in the scientific literature. The human CA1 protein contains an N-terminal active site, a zinc-binding site, and a substrate-binding site. The crystal structure of the human CA1-bicarbonate anion complex reveals the geometry of two hydrogen bonds: one between the Glu106-Thr199 pair and another between the Glu117-His119 pair. Additionally, there is a pi hydrogen bond between a water molecule and the phenyl ring of the Tyr114 residue. Product inhibition of CA1 by bicarbonate anions is associated with a change in proton localization on His119. The Glu117-His119 hydrogen bond is thought to regulate the ionic properties of the zinc ion and the binding strength of the bicarbonate anion. CA1 belongs to the α-CA subfamily and is localized in the cytosol of red blood cells, the gastrointestinal tract, cardiac tissues, and other organs or tissues. The transmembrane transport of bicarbonate produced by CA1 plays a significant role in cellular pH regulation. A zinc-activated variant of CA1, known as the Michigan Variant, involves a single point mutation that changes His67 to Arg in a critical region of the active site. This variant exhibits unique esterase activity that is specifically enhanced by the addition of free zinc ions. Activation of CA1 has been associated with worsened pathological remodeling in ischemic diabetic cardiomyopathy. In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and post-infarct heart failure undergoing surgical coronary revascularization, myocardial levels of CA1 were found to be sixfold higher than in non-diabetic patients. Elevated CA1 expression was primarily localized in the cardiac interstitium and endothelial cells. Furthermore, high glucose-induced elevation of CA1 impairs endothelial cell permeability and induces endothelial cell apoptosis in vitro. CA1 also mediates hemorrhagic retinal and cerebral vascular permeability through prekallikrein activation and the generation of serine protease factor XIIa. These processes contribute to the progression of proliferative diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema, which are leading causes of vision loss. Given its clinical significance, CA1 is considered an important therapeutic target, and the development of its inhibitors could aid in disease treatment. Compared to other members of the CA family, CA1 has relatively low affinity for common CA inhibitors but exhibits medium affinity for sulfonamide-based CA inhibitors.
